title: Nvidia, AMD and Micron Lead Chip Rebound After Worst Selloff Since 2020
headline: Nvidia, AMD and Micron Lead Chip Rebound After Worst Selloff Since 2020
subheadline: AMD closed up 11%, Intel 8% and Micron 5% on Friday, recovering only part of a November 5 rout in which the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25%, its steepest drop since March 2020.
summary: AMD closed up 11%, Intel 8% and Micron 5% on Friday, recovering only part of a November 5 rout in which the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25%, its steepest drop since March 2020.
excerpt: AMD closed up 11%, Intel 8% and Micron 5% on Friday, recovering only part of a November 5 rout in which the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25%, its steepest drop since March 2020.
body:
• Chip stocks rebounded on Friday from the sector's worst selloff in six years: AMD closed up 11% and Intel up 8%, Micron rose 5%, Nvidia gained 3% and SanDisk 4%, while Broadcom added less than 1%, MarketWatch reported.
  • The selloff being reversed was severe: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25% to 9,011.14 on November 5, its biggest one-day percentage drop since March 16, 2020, with Micron down 17.46%, AMD down 17.26% and Nvidia down 9.26% that day.
  • Reuters tied the selloff to fears of tighter AI regulation after Democrats won control of Congress, and analysts quoted by MarketWatch called Friday's bounce a reflex move after a "violent" selloff, not a resolution of the data-centre policy risk.
  • For investors, Friday recovered only part of Thursday's losses: a 5% rise in Micron, for example, offsets only a fraction of its 17.46% fall the day before.

US chip stocks rebounded on Friday, led by Advanced Micro Devices, Intel, Micron and Nvidia, a day after the semiconductor sector suffered its worst selloff in six years. Shares of AMD and Intel closed up 11% and 8% respectively, Micron Technology rose 5%, Nvidia and SanDisk gained 3% and 4%, and Broadcom added less than 1%, MarketWatch reported via Morningstar.

The selloff being reversed

Thursday's decline set the scale of Friday's bounce. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25% to 9,011.14 on November 5, its biggest one-day percentage drop since March 16, 2020; in Nasdaq's daily record back to 1994, only that 15.9% drop in 2020 was larger. Micron fell 17.46% and AMD fell 17.26% on the day, Lam Research lost 16.36%, Applied Materials lost 13.58%, Broadcom lost 10.43% and Nvidia fell 9.26%, according to index data compiled from Yahoo Finance and Nasdaq closes. The index closed 38.4% below its June 22 record close of 14,634.72, while still up 27.2% in 2026. Reuters tied the selloff to fears of tighter AI regulation after Democrats won control of Congress.

Why buyers came back

Analysts quoted by MarketWatch described Friday as a reaction to the size of the fall rather than a change in the underlying news. StoneX analyst Yi Fu Lee told MarketWatch that Thursday's "violent" selloff created an "obvious reflex opportunity" among AI-exposed chip stocks on Friday, noting that the iShares Semiconductor ETF SOXX fell 12% on Thursday while the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF IGV lost 4%. J. Gold Associates analyst Jack Gold told MarketWatch there was a "big overreaction" in the market to the Democrats sweeping the election.

"I think that the selloff was just too steep."

— Jack Gold, J. Gold Associates, to MarketWatch

There was also better-than-feared messaging on the policy front. MarketWatch reported that Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who had promised a tougher approach to data-centre regulation while campaigning, said she was not ruling data centres out. Gold said he expected politicians in Ohio and New York could also moderate their stances, and Mark Spindel of Pilot Wave Holdings told MarketWatch that Friday's rebound reflected the market separating concerns about AI capital spending, data-centre policy, inflation and higher rates that Thursday's move had compressed into one trade.

Why the relief may not hold

The same analysts warned against reading one session as a turning point. Stifel analyst Brian Chin labelled Friday's action a "volatility whipsaw" and said the uncertainty around future data-centre spending probably is not going away, which could keep stocks volatile for some time, although he added that the underlying appetite for artificial intelligence had not changed since the midterm elections and that the regulatory pathway had "become more tricky." Lior Prosor of Deep33 told MarketWatch that a temporary slowdown in the US data-centre buildout does not necessarily mean lower revenues for AI-exposed companies in coming quarters, because available capacity could serve demand elsewhere. Lee cautioned that it is not wise to make "irrational portfolio decisions" during a "violent tape."

What to watch next

The arithmetic alone argues for caution: Friday's gains recovered only part of Thursday's losses, and the index's own history offers no reliable guide, with the index higher one month after five of the six earlier one-day drops of at least 10% in records back to 1994, by a median gain of 11.2%, but lower six months later in all three cases from 2000 to 2002. What matters next is sourced and specific: whether data-centre policy statements from incoming officeholders harden into actual restrictions, and whether chip companies' next earnings reports confirm the AI demand analysts say has not disappeared. Until then, Friday's session is best read as dip-buying after a historic fall, not as evidence that the fall's cause has been resolved.
